    On /record/update, every field named in Set is written and a field set to an empty string is taken off — the same rule the property endpoint follows. SetName with Name renames the heading; SetNotes with Notes replaces the body.

    Deleting a record is /delete with its hash, like any other heading: a record is a heading and nothing about it needs a delete of its own.

    Importing contacts from Apple, Google or Outlook

    Export a vCard (.vcf) file - Apple Contacts: select the people, File → Export → Export vCard; Google Contacts: Export → vCard - and import it:

    orgs contact import contacts.vcf -dry-run     what would happen, nothing written
orgs contact import contacts.vcf              add the new, fill in the known
orgs contact import contacts.vcf -mode skip   leave people already here alone
orgs contact import old.vcf -mode overwrite   the card wins where they differ

    or use the Import button on worg's Contacts tab, which shows the same plan before anything is written.

    A person is recognised by the card's UID (kept as VCARD_UID), then by any email address, then by name. The default, merge, never changes a value you have: it adds what is missing, files a second email beside the first (EMAIL_WORK_2), and tells you about a birthday or company that differs rather than writing it. Notes are appended only when they are new, so importing the same file again changes nothing. Photos are saved in images/contacts/ beside the org file and linked from IMAGE, and each record's history says the change came from the import.

    The card's fields become EMAIL, EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE, PHONE_HOME, FAX_WORK, ADDRESS_HOME, BIRTHDAY (--05-15 when the year is not known), ANNIVERSARY, COMPANY, DEPARTMENT, TITLE, NICKNAME, WEBSITE, LINKEDIN / TWITTER / GITHUB and the other networks, IM_SKYPE, RELATED_SPOUSE, and a custom label becomes the field's label (EMAIL_OLD_WORK). Categories become tags.

    How the writing works, and why

    Every write here is a line edit on the file rather than a rewrite of the parsed document. A record usually shares its file with a hundred others and with whatever else is in there, and writing the document back through go-org would reformat all of it — every drawer re-indented, every table reflowed — to change one phone number.

    Three things follow from that and are worth knowing before changing it:

    1. The drawers are found by walking the lines under the headline, not by asking go-org. A drawer written in column zero ends the headline's body as far as the parser is concerned and hoists the rest of the heading to the top of the document, where looking for it is guesswork.
    2. After any edit that changes how many lines a record has, its range is found again rather than adjusted. Keeping half a dozen indices in step through an insert, a delete and a rename is how off-by-one bugs get written.
    3. The property drawer is re-aligned after an edit. It is cosmetic and nothing reads the padding back — but a record is a text file somebody opens in an editor, and a ragged column is what "written by a program" looks like.

    Records And Collections

    A record is one heading that stands for one thing - a person, a laptop, a playing card - and keeps what is known about it in its property drawer. The heading is the thing's name, the properties are its fields, the body under it is whatever anybody wanted to write about it, and the LOGBOOK drawer is the history of what has been changed.

    What makes a heading a record

    One property, and nothing else:

    :RECORD: contact

    The value names the collection the record belongs to. contact is just the collection this was built for first; equipment, cards, wine and synths are records in exactly the same sense and are read by exactly the same code. A heading with no RECORD property is not a record, wherever it sits, and a heading with one is a record even if it sits on its own in the middle of a project file - which is what makes a record identifiable without any knowledge of where it lives.

    A contact

    * John Doe
  :PROPERTIES:
  :RECORD:       contact
  :ID:           b1d1a2f4-3c58-4f2a-9a3d-0f9a1c7e51aa
  :ADDED:        [2026-09-26 Sat 09:12]
  :EMAIL:        john.doe@example.com
  :EMAIL_WORK:   jdoe@acme.example.com
  :PHONE_MOBILE: +1-555-555-0199
  :PHONE_HOME:   +1-555-555-0100
  :ADDRESS:      123 Main St, Cityville
  :BIRTHDAY:     1990-05-15
  :IMAGE:        [[file:images/contacts/john-doe.jpg]]
  :LINKEDIN:     https://www.linkedin.com/in/johndoe
  :END:
  :LOGBOOK:
  - Updated [2026-09-26 Sat 14:02] EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE
  :END:

  Met at the 2019 conference. Allergic to shellfish.

    Fields, and how a field knows what it is

    A field is a property named NAME or NAME_LABEL. The label is free text and is how a thing has more than one of something: PHONE_MOBILE, PHONE_HOME and PHONE_WORK are three phone numbers, EMAIL and EMAIL_WORK are two email addresses. Nothing has to be declared first.

    What a field is is worked out from the part before the label, so a client draws a field by its kind and never needs a list of property names:

    Name Kind Drawn as
    EMAIL, MAIL email a mailto: link
    PHONE, MOBILE, CELL, TEL, FAX tel a tel: link
    ADDRESS, ADDR postal text, with a map link
    URL, WEBSITE, HOMEPAGE, LINK, BLOG url a link
    LINKEDIN, FACEBOOK, TWITTER, GITHUB, … social the network's own badge
    BIRTHDAY, ANNIVERSARY, and anything *_DATE date a date, and on the agenda
    IMAGE, PHOTO, AVATAR, PORTRAIT, PICTURE, LOGO image the picture itself
    anything else text as written

    The social names are a list rather than a rule because that is what they are; see socialNetworks below to add one. Everything else is a rule, so a collection of guitar pedals gets MANUAL_URL drawn as a link and BOUGHT_DATE drawn as a date without anybody teaching it anything.

    The bookkeeping fields

    Property Written by Means
    RECORD you or us which collection this belongs to - the identity
    ID us a uuid, so links and other records can point here
    ADDED us when the record was first written down

    They are kept out of the field list a client is handed, because they are about the record rather than about the thing.

    The history

    Every change made through the record endpoints prepends a line to the heading's LOGBOOK drawer:

    :LOGBOOK:
- Updated [2026-09-26 Sat 14:02] EMAIL_WORK, PHONE_MOBILE
- Renamed [2026-09-26 Sat 13:55] John Doe
- Added [2026-09-26 Sat 09:12]
:END:

    Newest first, the way org writes a logbook. The clock entries org puts in the same drawer are left alone and ignored, and a line somebody writes by hand that does not match is skipped rather than being a parse error.

    Collections

    A collection is every record sharing one RECORD value. It does not have to be declared - the first heading with :RECORD: wine: on it makes the wine collection exist - but a container gives new records somewhere to go and gives the collection a name and an icon:

    * Contacts
  :PROPERTIES:
  :COLLECTION: contact
  :ICON:       👤
  :FIELDS:     EMAIL, PHONE_MOBILE, ADDRESS, BIRTHDAY, IMAGE
  :END:

    FIELDS is the order an add form should offer, not a restriction: a record may carry anything. Where there is no container the server offers the fields the records of that type already use, commonest first.

    Duplicating an entry

    Copy the heading, change the name, change the values, and delete the ID and ADDED lines - the server fills those in the next time it writes to the record, and two records with the same ID is the one thing that will confuse a link. Nothing else about a record is derived, so a record written by hand in a text editor is the same as one added from worg.

    Settings

    Aliases

    This is a command line tool helper. These are stored prefixes for long command lines that are repetitive. Aliases provide a means of shortening command lines to common patterns Ex: If you alway refile from a particular inbox file you can add something as follows to your orgs.yaml and tri will expand to the source from your inbox file:

      aliases:
    triage: ["ref" "-from" "inbox.org"]

    Any additional parameters will end up after the alias

    Attachments

    Files that belong to a heading - a pdf, a photograph of a whiteboard, a spreadsheet somebody sent - kept the way org-attach keeps them.

    attach:
  dir: "data"
  tag: "ATTACH"
  maxMb: 64

    Nothing here is required; every value above is the default.

    dir is where a heading's folder is made, relative to your first orgDir. A heading's folder is that directory, then the first two characters of its :ID:, then the rest of it - data/8f/3c1a20-.../ - which is exactly what emacs' org-attach does, so a database written by either is readable by the other.

    A heading can also name its own folder with a :DIR: property (or the older :ATTACH_DIR:), which is read relative to the org file that holds the heading. A heading with one of those does not need an :ID: and will not be given one.

    tag is put on a heading the first time something is attached to it, so that IsTask() && HasTags("ATTACH") finds everything with a file on it. Set it to an empty string to tag nothing.

    maxMb is the biggest single upload that will be taken.

    Clock Into Drawer

    When using the clocking features org can choose to dump clock data at the top of a heading OR produce the clock data into a drawer of your choosing. This option lets you choose the name of the drawer.

     clockIntoDrawer: "LOGBOOK"

    This defaults to LOGBOOK

    Column View

    #+COLUMNS: is org's way of saying "show me these properties as a table", and the part that makes it more than a table is that a column may ask for a total: %EFFORT{:} makes a project heading show the effort of everything under it.

    columns:
  default: "%ITEM %TODO %PRIORITY %TAGS %EFFORT{:} %CLOCKSUM"

    This is used only for a file that does not declare a #+COLUMNS: line of its own; one that does gets exactly what it asked for. The built-in default is org's own columns (%ITEM %TODO %PRIORITY %TAGS, without org's terminal widths so worg shares the screen between them) with %EFFORT{:} %CLOCKSUM added, because adding effort up is the thing this view exists for and nearly no file declares a columns line.

    Date Tree Formatting

    These options control the format of your datatree

     * 2006
 ** January
 *** 01 Monday
     * 2006
 ** 2006-01 October
 *** 2006-01-02 Friday
 *** 2006-01-02 Saturday
    dateTreeYearFormat:  "2006"
dateTreeMonthFormat: "January"
dateTreeDayFormat:   "01 Monday"

    Day Page

    The day page system has a number of settings that can be used to control its behaviour.

    The first and most important is where your daypages should be generated This should be a folder inside your orgDirs.

     dayPagePath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/worklog"

    Default Author

    Default author parameter to use when generating new templates

     author: "John Smith"

    Dnd Paths

    Where the dnd module looks for ruleset yaml modules (extra races, classes, backgrounds, spells or whole homebrew rulesets). The built in SRD data is always loaded first, these directories are merged on top.

     dndPaths:
   - "/Users/me/dnd/homebrew"

    When this is empty the module still searches <templatePath>/dnd, ./templates/dnd (or, when neither exists, the dnd folder built into the binary) and ~/.orgs/dnd.

    Dnd Session Path

    Where play session logs are written. Starting a session from a character sheet creates a dated org file in this folder and every roll you make and note you take is appended to it.

     dndSessionPath: "/Users/me/dev/gtd/dndsessions"
 dndSessionTemplate: "dndsession.tpl"

    A relative path is taken relative to your first orgDir, and when the setting is left out entirely the folder is <orgDir>/dndsessions. Keep it inside an orgDir so that the sessions land in your org database and can be searched, agenda'd and archived like everything else.

    Enabled Exporters, Plugins, Updaters

    The list of enabled exporter modules

    exporters:
   - name: "gantt"
   - name: "mermaid"
   - name: "mindmap"
   - name: "html"
     props:
       fontfamily: "Underdog"
   - name: "revealjs"
   - name: "impressjs"
   - name: "latex"

    The same is true for updaters and plugins. You must explicitly enable the modules you wish to be active in your orgs installation for them to be available.

    Encryption

    A heading tagged :crypt: whose body is ciphertext on disk - org-crypt's format exactly, so a heading encrypted here opens in emacs and one encrypted in emacs opens here.

    crypt:
  key: ""             # a gpg key id. Empty means symmetric.
  tag: "crypt"
  bin: ""             # the gpg binary, found on PATH when empty
  unlockSeconds: 0

    Nothing here is required and there is nothing to turn on: if gpg is installed, /crypt/* works. GET /crypt/config says which mode it is in and how many tagged headings are still sitting in the clear.

    What this protects, and what it does not. It protects the file - a backup, a sync folder, a git remote, a stolen disk - and every part of this server that reads org files without going through the crypt endpoints: the search index, grep, the link graph, every exporter. None of them had to be taught to keep a secret, because there is no secret in what they read.

    It does not on its own protect against somebody who can reach the server. That is a question about who holds the key, which is why the server holds no passphrase: one arrives with the request that needs it, is handed to gpg down a pipe, and is forgotten.

    key is the arrangement worth having on a server other machines can reach. With a public key the server encrypts with no secret at all and cannot decrypt, whatever is done to it - decryption needs the private key, which lives where you keep it. A heading can name its own with a :CRYPTKEY: property, as org-crypt does.

    unlockSeconds holds a passphrase in memory for that long so it does not have to be retyped. It is off by default and is a number rather than a switch because it trades the property above away: for those seconds, reaching the server is enough.

    Filters

    Filters provide a built in set of expressions that can be used to filter your org mode headings. By default adding to filters in your config file will add new or override internal ones. If you find the internal list to be annoying you can simply turn on

       noInternalfilters: true

    Which will cause the internal filters to not be defined.

        "filters":
    	"alltasks": "!IsProject() && IsTodo() && !IsArchived() && !InTagGroup('PERSONAL')",

    Filters can be used as a macro in a query using handlebars style notation in the query passed to the server.

        	"query": "{{ alltasks }}",

    Go Links

    Where orgs gocap files a link, and the heading it goes under. Both are optional; these are the defaults.

    server:
  goLinksFile:    "links.org"
  goLinksHeading: "Links"

    The file is relative to the first of the orgDirs. It is the built in GoLink capture template's target, so a capture template of your own called GoLink replaces the whole thing.

    Image Path

    Images and fonts are secondary html requests when loading an html document in vscode. In addition, orgs may want to provide quick links et al.

     templateImagesPath: "<path>"
 templateFontPath: "<path>"

    This defaults to: ./templates/html_styles/images

    The images and fonts built into the binary are served behind these folders, so either may be left out; a file of the same name in the folder replaces the built in one.

    Inbox Triage and the Weekly Review

    What orgs triage, orgs review week and worg's Inbox and Weekly Review tabs treat as the inbox, as someday, and as waiting:

    review:
  inbox: 'InFile("(^|/)inbox[.]org$") && !IsArchived() && !IsDone()'
  somedayKeywords: [SOMEDAY, MAYBE]
  somedayTags: [someday, maybe]
  waiting: 'IsStatus("WAITING") && !IsArchived()'
  waitingDays: 7

    Every key may be left out; the values above are the defaults. Only the outermost heading a query finds is an item - the headings under it go wherever it goes.

    Link Protocols

    Teach orgs your own link protocols. A link written [[jira:ABC-123]] (or jira://ABC-123) is then followed wherever you say: either to a real url, or by running a tool of yours on it.

    server:
  linkProtocols:
    jira:
      urlPrefix: "https://mycompany.atlassian.net/browse/"
    wiki:
      url: "https://wiki.me.com/pages/{{path}}/view"
    rdar:
      cmd: "mytool --open {{link}}"
    ticket:
      cmd: "tkt show"
      withProtocol: true
    • urlPrefix replaces the protocol: jira:ABC-123 becomes https://mycompany.atlassian.net/browse/ABC-123.
    • url splices the link into a url, for when it does not go at the end.
    • cmd is a command line to run. {{link}} is the whole link, protocol included; {{path}} is what comes after the protocol. With neither, the path is added as the last argument, or the whole link when withProtocol is set.

    The server works out where a link goes and hands it back (GET /links/resolve, and Open / Command on /links/all); a command is run by the client following the link, never by the server. orgs go follows them, and orgs go jira:ABC-123 follows a link typed straight in.

    Logging

    TODO: Fill in information on orgs server logging

    Login Lifetime

    How long a login lasts before it has to be renewed. A Go duration, plus d for days and w for weeks; one hour when not set.

     tokenExpiry: "8h"     # or "30m", "7d", "2w", "1d12h"

    The command line renews its token on its own while the old one is still good, so this is mostly how long a token copied somewhere else stays useful - and how long a stolen one would.

    Marking Something Done

    Org does three things when a heading reaches a DONE keyword, and orgs used to do none of them: it stamps CLOSED:, it writes a line saying which state the heading moved from and when, and - if the heading repeats - it moves the repeating date on instead of leaving the keyword sitting on DONE forever.

    These are the same three switches org has, under the same names, and they can be set here, per file with #+STARTUP:, or per heading with a :LOGGING: property. The narrowest one that says anything wins.

    log:
  done: "time"          # none | time | note
  repeat: "time"        # none | time | note
  intoDrawer: "LOGBOOK" # a drawer name, or "" to write into the body
  states: false         # log every state change, not only done ones
  repeatToState: ""     # a keyword, "previous", or "" for the first one

    done is org's org-log-done. time stamps CLOSED: and writes a State "DONE" from "NEXT" [...] line; note does the same and keeps a note with it; none does neither. repeat is org-log-repeat and says what to write when a repeating date moves on - a repeat is not a closure, so no CLOSED: is stamped and any existing one is taken off.

    intoDrawer is org-log-into-drawer. A name puts the lines in that drawer; empty writes them into the body as a plain list, which is what org does by default. It defaults to LOGBOOK here rather than to nothing, because the agenda's habit graph is built by reading those lines back out of LOGBOOK and can only work if that is where they go.

    states logs every change between keywords rather than only the ones into a DONE state. Per-keyword cookies in a #+TODO: line say the same thing for one keyword and always win: NEXT(n!) logs a timestamp on entering NEXT whatever states says, and WAITING(w@) keeps a note.

    repeatToState is org-todo-repeat-to-state: which keyword a repeating heading goes back to. Empty means the first keyword of the sequence, which is what org does; previous means whichever state it was in before it was marked done; anything else is used as the keyword.

    At the file level, the #+STARTUP: words org defines all work: logdone, nologdone, lognotedone, logrepeat, nologrepeat, lognoterepeat, logdrawer and nologdrawer. So does #+PROPERTY: LOG_INTO_DRAWER, and a heading's own :LOG_INTO_DRAWER: or :LOGGING: property.

    Org Dirs

    A list of directories containing your org files

     orgDirs:
   - "/Users/me/dev/gtd"

    Orgs Keys

    There are 2 keys that will be generated if not provided by the system.

     orgJWS: "this key is used to sign the JWT"
 orgJWE: "This key is used to encrypt the JWT"
 orgSalt: "Appended to the per user salt to help with rainbow tables"

    Orgs Keystore

    Orgs has various ways of storing credentials. You need something to protect your data. By default the yaml keystore is just a file with usernames and creds. Other keystores are possible.

     keystore: "path to yaml file"

    A relative path is taken relative to this configuration file. Until you set this, the only account that exists is admin/default and the server says so loudly on every startup. Add accounts with orgs user add; see "Users and the keystore" for the whole of it.

    Running Source Blocks

    Orgs can run the #+BEGIN_SRC blocks in your files and hand the result back - what org calls babel. It is off unless you turn it on, and that is deliberate: a source block is somebody else's program, the server may be reachable from anything on your network, and noAuth is a setting people use. Reading your files and running them are different promises.

    babel:
  enable: true
  languages: ["python", "sh", "emacs-lisp"]
  timeout: 30

    languages is an allow list. Empty means every language orgs knows how to run, which is the shorter way of saying yes to all of them. The names are the ones you write after #+BEGIN_SRC, and the aliases go with them - allowing python allows py too.

    timeout is in seconds and is a wall clock limit on one block, so a loop that never ends costs half a minute rather than the server.

    commands replaces how a language is run, for an interpreter that is not on the path or one orgs does not know:

    babel:
  enable: true
  commands:
    python: ["/usr/local/bin/python3.12"]
    julia: ["julia", "--startup-file=no"]

    The code is handed to the command on standard input.

    Tag Groups

    Tag Groups are a cheater way of helping to make your queries less verbose. They are defined on the orgs server and provide a grouping of tags that you can query against.

    Here is a quick example. The following entry in your orgs.yaml allows you to treat PERSONAL as any of FAMILY ME or PERSONAL tags and WORK as any of WORK BACKLOG or PROJECTX tags in an InTagGroup('GROUPNAME') query.

    tagGroups:
 PERSONAL:
   - FAMILY
   - ME
   - PERSONAL
 WORK:
   - WORK
   - BACKLOG
   - PROJECTX

    By default ORGS turns on tag groups that I find most useful If you would like to avoid those being defined turn on the following flag

       noInternalTagGroups: true

    Here is a query that might be using that in your vscode org.todoConfigs: I am defining a Todo view that will have filename, status, headline and a few property columns of various sizes and it is looking for active todo's that are either WAITING or BLOCKED that are not tagged with any tags in my PERSONAL tag group.

      "Waiting": {
    "query": "!IsProject() && IsTodo() && !IsArchived() && !InTagGroup('PERSONAL') && (IsStatus('WAITING') || IsStatus('BLOCKED')",
    "display": {
      "filename": 15,
      "status": 10,
      "headline": 25,
      "properties": {
        "EFFORT": 5,
        "ASSIGNED": 15
      }
    }
  }

    The Agenda

    GET /agenda works out what lands on each day (repeaters, ranges, overdue items carried to today, deadline warnings). A deadline starts showing on today this many days before it is due, unless its stamp names its own warning period (<2026-10-20 Tue -3d>):

    agenda:
  deadlineWarningDays: 14

    Unset is org's own 14. 0 shows a deadline only on its day (and as overdue after it).

    Update Check

    GET /version tells a client (the vscode plugin, orgs version) which version this server is and whether a newer release is out. To know that, the server asks github for the latest release of ihdavids/orgs, at most every six hours. Turn the question off with:

     noUpdateCheck: true

    Use Project Tag

    How should we define a project. If this is set a project is defined as a heading with a :PROJECT: tag on it.

     useProjectTag: true

    If this is false then a project is defined to be a headline that has a child headline that has a status on it.

     * Project
 ** TODO This task makes it a project

    Users and the keystore

    Orgs keeps its users in a keystore file, named by keystore: in the server block of your config. A relative path is taken relative to the configuration file itself, the same way orgs_extensions.yaml is.

    server:
  keystore: "orgs_keystore.yaml"

    Until you set this, the only account that exists is admin/default, which is built in so that a fresh server can be logged into at all. The server prints a large warning on startup for as long as that is true.

    Users are added with the orgs user command, which reads the same config file the server does and writes the keystore beside it:

    orgs user add ian          # prompts for a password, twice
orgs user ls               # who exists, and how their password is stored
orgs user passwd ian       # change one
orgs user rm ian           # remove one

    The command edits a file on disk, so it has to be run on the machine the server runs on. It never talks to the server, and the server picks the change up the next time it starts.

    Administrators, and adding a user over the wire

    An account marked admin: true may add another account without having access to the server's disk, which is what orgs adduser does:

    orgs adduser dana          # prompts for a password, twice
orgs adduser sam -admin    # and this one may add users too

    Unlike orgs user, this talks to the server (POST /users/add), so it works from anywhere you can log in - and the new account works at once rather than at the next restart, because the server writes the keystore it is already holding.

    The password still never travels: the client makes a salt for the new user and sends ClientHash of the password under it, the same as a login does.

    Somebody has to be an administrator before any of this can be used, and the only account that starts out as one is the built-in admin. On a keystore written by hand, or by a version of orgs older than this, mark one on the server's own machine:

    orgs user admin ian        # ian may now add users
orgs user noadmin ian      # and now may not
orgs user add dana -admin  # added as an administrator

    The server will not add a user when it is running on its built-in admin/default account, because that keystore has no file behind it and there would be nowhere to write. It says so rather than appearing to work.

    The file it writes looks like this - the password is a hash, and the salt is per user:

    creds:
  ian:
    password: "sha256:9f2c..."
    salt: "b3d1..."
logins:
  ian: 2026-09-30T11:04:17Z

    A password: written out as cleartext still works, so a keystore typed by hand does what it looks like it does - but the server names those accounts in its startup warning, and orgs user passwd is how to convert one.

    Passwords are never sent to the server. A client asks for the user's salt, hashes the password with it, and sends the hash; the server hashes that again with orgSalt before comparing. Set requireHashedLogin: true to refuse a login that arrives as cleartext at all - worth doing once every client talking to this server is new enough to hash, and noted in the startup warning until then.

    Voice Notes

    Recording and transcription. Orgs does not transcribe anything itself - it runs a go-whisper server, hands it the recording, and files what comes back as an org heading.

    Two settings turn the whole thing on: where the models are, and the port to run whisper on.

     voice:
   models: "/Users/me/whisper/models"
   port: 8081

    With those, orgs starts gowhisper itself when the server starts and stops it when the server stops. The binary is looked for on your PATH and in the usual places; bin says where it is when it is somewhere else. Something already listening on that port is adopted rather than started again, so a whisper you run by hand still works.

    Everything else has a default worth leaving alone:

     voice:
   models: "/Users/me/whisper/models"
   port: 8081
   bin: "/usr/local/bin/gowhisper"   # when it is not on PATH
   gpu: true                          # let whisper use the GPU
   args: []                           # anything else for its command line
   url: "http://otherbox:8081"        # a whisper orgs does not start
   model: "ggml-medium-q5_0"          # empty asks the server for its first
   language: "en"                     # empty lets whisper detect it
   dir: "audio"                       # recordings, relative to your orgDir
   timeout: 600                       # seconds to wait for a transcription
   maxMb: 64                          # the largest single recording
   tags:
     - "voice"
   target:
     type: "file+headline"
     filename: "inbox.org"
     id: "Voice Notes"

    model is the model id to transcribe with - when it is empty orgs asks the server what it has and uses the first, which is right for a machine with one model installed and wrong as soon as there are two.

    dir is where recordings are kept, relative to your first orgDir, so that a note's audio sits in the org database beside the heading that links to it. timeout is how long to wait for a transcription - a long take on a large model is minutes, not seconds.

    target is where a voice note is filed when the client does not say, and takes the same shape as a capture template's target. tags are put on every voice note heading.

    Tables

    Details

    Table formulas — a spreadsheet in an org table

    What this is

    An org table can carry formulas on a #+TBLFM: line under it. The server works them out and writes the answers back into the table's cells, so a table of expenses can total itself, a reading list can count what is finished, and an order sheet can look prices up in another table.

    This is not Emacs' table engine. Emacs hands formulas to Calc or Lisp, which a server cannot run, so orgs has its own expression language with the same cell references ($3, @2$3, @2$1..@>$1) and its own function library. Plain arithmetic formulas usually work in both; anything using the functions below works only here.

    Every example in this guide is run by the test suite (internal/app/orgs/tablesguide_test.go): the tables are shown with the answers the evaluator really produces.

    Running the formulas

    Nothing is recalculated as you type. Formulas run when you ask:

    • terminal: orgs tables eval NAME (orgs tables lists the tables and their names)
    • worg: the Tables tab, saving a table with evaluation on
    • VS Code: Org: Execute Table with the cursor in the table, or Org: Execute All Tables In File

    The table is rewritten in place, realigned, with the formula line kept.

    If a formula fails, nothing is written and the error names the formula.

    Anatomy of a formula
    | item   | qty | price | total |
|--------+-----+-------+-------|
| apples |   3 |  0.50 |  1.50 |
| pears  |   2 |  1.25 |  2.50 |
| plums  |  10 |  0.20 |  2.00 |
|--------+-----+-------+-------|
| total  |  15 |       |  6.00 |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2*$3;%.2f::@>$2=vsum(@2$2..@4$2)::@>$4=vsum(@2$4..@4$4);%.2f

    The #+TBLFM: line holds any number of formulas separated by ::, run left to right, so a later formula sees what an earlier one wrote. Each is

    target=expression;format

    Here $4=$2*$3 fills every row of column 4 with quantity times price. It runs on the total row too (giving 0, since that row has no price), and then @>$4…= overwrites that one cell with the sum.

    Naming cells: rows and columns
    Reference Means
    $3 column 3. As a target: every row but the header
    @2$3 row 2, column 3
    @>$3 the last row, column 3. @< is the first row
    @2$1..@4$3 a rectangle of cells, read row by row
    @-1$3 one row up from the row being filled (@+1 down)
    @#, $# the number of the row or column being filled
    remote(Name, $2) column 2 of the table named Name (see Other tables)

    Rows are counted without the separator lines: @1 is the header, @2 the first row under the first line, and a second line further down adds nothing to the count. In the example above the total row is @5.

    When a table has a header (a separator line after its first row), the header is never written to and is left out of column ranges.

    The format after the semicolon

    Everything after ; says how the answer is written and how cells are read.

    Part Effect
    %.2f a printf pattern for the answer: %.2f two decimals, %5.1f padded to 5 characters
    %d a whole number; the fraction is dropped, not rounded: 4.5 is written 4 (as Emacs does)
    N read every cell as a number: text counts as 0, true as 1, a lone empty cell as 0
    E keep empty cells in ranges; without it vsum, vmean, vcount skip them
    $ money: $ is stripped from cells when reading and put in front of the answer
    H include the header row in column ranges

    They combine: ;%.2f$ writes $12.50.

    | item   | price | qty |   cost |
|--------+-------+-----+--------|
| tea    | $2.50 |   2 |  $5.00 |
| coffee | $4.25 |   3 | $12.75 |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2*$3;%.2f$

    E and N in action; column 1 has an empty cell and a word:

    | x   | counted | counted, E | mean | mean, N |
|-----+---------+------------+------+---------|
| 4   |       3 |          4 |    6 |       4 |
|     |         |            |      |         |
| 8   |         |            |      |         |
| n/a |         |            |      |         |
#+TBLFM: @2$2=vcount($1)::@2$3=vcount($1);E::@2$4=vmean($1)::@2$5=vmean($1);N

    vcount counts the three filled cells, or all four with E. vmean averages the numbers and passes over the text: (4+8)/2. With N the text n/a becomes a 0, so it is (4+8+0)/3; the empty cell is still left out, because leaving empty cells out is what E changes, not N.

    Named columns, named cells and parameters

    A table whose first column is a marker column can name things, as in Emacs. The marker in the first cell says what the row is:

    Marker Row holds
    ! column names: $qty then means $3 (the marker column is column 1)
    ^ names for the cells just above it: $subtotal means that cell
    _ names for the cells just below it
    $ parameters, written name=value: $rate is that value

    Rows with a marker are never written to by formulas.

    |   | item | qty | price | total |
|---+------+-----+-------+-------|
| ! | item | qty | price | total |
|   | tea  |   2 |   2.5 |     5 |
|   | jam  |   1 |     4 |     4 |
#+TBLFM: $5=$qty*$price
    |   |  net | tax |
|---+------+-----|
|   |  100 |  20 |
|   |   50 |  10 |
| $ | rate=0.2 |     |
#+TBLFM: $3=$2*$rate

    A parameter is read like a cell, so rate=0.2 is the number 0.2. The $ row is a row of the table like any other, so a whole-column range (vsum($2)) would take its cell in too.

    Constants

    #+CONSTANTS: vat=0.2 shop=Corner in the file makes $vat and $shop available to every table in it, and a heading's properties are there as $PROP_NAME. Constants are text, not numbers: wrap them in value() to calculate with them.

    #+CONSTANTS: vat=0.2
| net | with vat |
|-----+----------|
| 100 |      120 |
|  50 |       60 |
#+TBLFM: $2=$1*(1+value($vat))
    What a cell's value is

    Before a formula sees a cell, its text is read as the first of these that fits:

    1. empty: an empty value (0 with N)
    2. a number: 42, -3.5, 1e3 (with $, $12.50 too)
    3. a date: <2026-10-02 Fri>, <2026-10-02 Fri 09:30>, [2026-10-02 Fri], 2026-10-02, 2026-10-02 09:30
    4. a duration: 1:30, 2h, 1d 4h, 3w (a week is five days, as for effort estimates)
    5. true or false: t, true, TRUE, True and f, false …
    6. otherwise text
    | cell             | number | date  | text  | blank |
|------------------+--------+-------+-------+-------|
| 42               | true   | false | false | false |
| <2026-10-02 Fri> | false  | true  | false | false |
| hello            | false  | false | true  | false |
| TRUE             | false  | false | false | false |
|                  | false  | false | false | true  |
#+TBLFM: $2=isnumber($1)::$3=isdate($1)::$4=istext($1)::$5=isblank($1)

    An answer is written as: numbers as short as they can be (3, not 3.000000, unless a format says otherwise); dates as <2026-10-02 Fri>, with the time only when it is not midnight; durations as 1d 2h 30mins; true and false as true and false; a list as [1 2 3] (use join to write one nicely).

    In a formula, text goes in quotes, single or double: 'fruit', "fruit". true, false, t, f and pi are names you can use directly.

    How a function reads its arguments

    This is the rule to remember. A cell reference means one of two things, and which one depends on the function, not on how you wrote it:

    • where a function wants a range (vsum and the other v functions, vsumif and the criteria functions, the ranges of a lookup, join, sort), $2 is the whole column, header left out;
    • where a function wants a value (sqrt, round, upper, concat, if, and, the dates, the value a lookup searches for), $2 is the cell in the row being filled.

    Each function's table below says which of its arguments are ranges: they are the ones named range, keys, results or values.

    | x | root | share |
|---+------+-------|
| 4 | 2.00 |  0.20 |
| 9 | 3.00 |  0.45 |
| 7 | 2.65 |  0.35 |
#+TBLFM: $2=sqrt($1);%.2f::$3=$1/vsum($1);%.2f

    In $1/vsum($1) the first $1 is this row's x and the second is every x: each row's share of the total. A rectangle like @2$1..@4$1 is always a range.

    Arithmetic and comparisons (+ - * / % **, < < > >= = !=, && || !, cond ? a : b) work on the current row's cells.

    Matching cells: criteria

    The if family of functions (vsumif, vcountif …) take a criteria argument saying which cells count:

    Criteria Matches
    'fruit' cells equal to fruit, ignoring case: Fruit, FRUIT
    5 or '5' cells equal to the number 5
    '>10' numbers over 10; also >=, <, <=
    '<>done' anything but done, including empty cells; != also works
    '>=2026-01-01' dates on or after the first of January 2026
    'app*' text starting app; * is any run of characters
    '?ale' four letters ending ale; ? is any one character
    '' or ''= empty cells
    '<>' cells that are not empty
    $1 cells equal to this row's cell in column 1

    A number never equals text, and > or < between a number and text is false. Text is ordered alphabetically, ignoring case.

    Conditional totals: the if functions
    Function Gives
    vsumif(range, criteria) the sum of the numbers in range that match
    vsumif(range, criteria, values) the sum of values on the rows where range matches
    vcountif(range, criteria) how many cells in range match
    vmeanif(range, criteria [, values]) the mean, as vsumif; 0 when nothing matches
    vmaxif, vminif(range, criteria [, values]) the largest or smallest, as vsumif; 0 when nothing matches
    vsumifs(values, range1, crit1, range2, crit2, ...) the sum of values on rows where every criterion matches
    vmeanifs(values, range1, crit1, ...) the mean, as vsumifs
    vcountifs(range1, crit1, range2, crit2, ...) rows where every criterion matches
    vcounta(range) cells that are not empty, whatever is in them
    vcountblank(range) empty cells

    The ranges are walked side by side, so range and values should be the same height: row 3 of one goes with row 3 of the other. Empty cells are kept in place for this (unlike vsum), and text in values is ignored.

    Note the argument order: vsumif puts the values last (optional), the ifs forms put them first (required), as spreadsheets do.

    | name          | kind  | qty | price |
|---------------+-------+-----+-------|
| apple         | fruit |   3 |   1.5 |
| pear          | fruit |   5 |     2 |
| kale          | veg   |   2 |     4 |
| beet          | veg   |     |     1 |
|---------------+-------+-----+-------|
| fruit qty     |       |   8 |       |
| veg rows      |       |   2 |       |
| qty over 2    |       |   8 |       |
| names p...    |       |   1 |       |
| fruit price   |       |     |  1.75 |
| dear fruit    |       |   5 |       |
| qty filled in |       |   3 |       |
| qty missing   |       |   1 |       |
#+TBLFM: @6$3=vsumif(@2$2..@5$2,'fruit',@2$3..@5$3)::@7$3=vcountif(@2$2..@5$2,'veg')::@8$3=vsumif(@2$3..@5$3,'>2')::@9$3=vcountif(@2$1..@5$1,'p*')::@10$4=vmeanif(@2$2..@5$2,'fruit',@2$4..@5$4)::@11$3=vsumifs(@2$3..@5$3,@2$2..@5$2,'fruit',@2$4..@5$4,'>1.5')::@12$3=vcounta(@2$3..@5$3)::@13$3=vcountblank(@2$3..@5$3)

    The summary rows sit in the same columns as the data, so these formulas use explicit rectangles (@2$3..@5$3). A whole column ($3) would take the summary rows in too.

    Looking things up
    Function Gives
    lookup(value, keys, results) the cell of results beside the first key equal to value
    lookupfirst(value, keys, results) the same as lookup
    lookuplast(value, keys, results) beside the last equal key
    lookupall(value, keys, results) every match, as a list
    index(range, n) the nth cell of range, from 1; -1 is the last, -2 the one before
    match(value, range) the position of the first cell equal to value, from 1; 0 when there is none
    • With no results, a lookup gives the matching key itself, as Emacs' org-lookup-first does (useful to ask "is it there?").
    • When nothing matches, lookup and lookuplast give an empty cell rather than an error, so one missing key doesn't stop the whole table.
    • Equal means as in criteria without an operator: numbers by value, text ignoring case, dates by date. Wildcards and operators are not used.
    • index past either end is an error, which stops the formula.

    The common case, a price list kept in its own table:

    #+NAME: Prices
| item   | price |
|--------+-------|
| tea    |   2.5 |
| coffee |     4 |
| jam    |   3.2 |
    | item   | qty | price | cost |
|--------+-----+-------+------|
| coffee |   2 |     4 |    8 |
| tea    |   3 |   2.5 |  7.5 |
| bread  |   1 |       |    0 |
#+TBLFM: $3=lookup($1,remote(Prices,$1),remote(Prices,$2))::$4=$2*$3

    Here $1 is read as a value (this row's item) and the two remote(...) as whole columns of Prices. Bread is not in the price list, so its price is left empty, and an empty cell counts as 0 in the arithmetic.

    The others, over one table:

    | day | who  | hours |
|-----+------+-------|
| mon | ann  |     3 |
| tue | bob  |     5 |
| wed | ann  |     2 |
|-----+------+-------|
| ann first   |   |     3 |
| ann last    |   |     2 |
| ann all     |   |   3,2 |
| bob is at   |   |     2 |
| second day  |   |   tue |
| last hours  |   |     2 |
#+TBLFM: @5$3=lookup('ann',@2$2..@4$2,@2$3..@4$3)::@6$3=lookuplast('ann',@2$2..@4$2,@2$3..@4$3)::@7$3=join(',',lookupall('ann',@2$2..@4$2,@2$3..@4$3))::@8$3=match('bob',@2$2..@4$2)::@9$3=index(@2$1..@4$1,2)::@10$3=index(@2$3..@4$3,-1)

    A lookup's value can also be this row's cell, so each row can find something about itself: $4=lookuplast($2,$2,$3) puts, beside every row, the hours of the last row for the same person.

    Statistics
    Function Gives
    vsum, vmean, vmedian total, average, middle value
    vmin, vmax smallest and largest; 0 when there are no numbers
    vcount (or vlen) how many cells are filled in (numbers, text, anything)
    vprod all the numbers multiplied together; 0 when there are none
    vsdev, vvar standard deviation and variance of a sample (divides by n-1), like STDEV, VAR
    vpsdev, vpvar of a whole population (divides by n), like STDEV.P, VAR.P
    vmode the number that occurs most often; on a tie, the one that comes first
    vpercentile(range, p) the value p of the way up: p from 0 to 1, or 0 to 100; interpolates like PERCENTILE.INC
    vquartile(range, q) q = 0 smallest, 1 first quartile, 2 median, 3 third quartile, 4 largest
    vrank(value, range) 1 for the largest number in range, 2 for the next …; equal numbers share a rank
    vrank(value, range, true) 1 for the smallest instead

    All of these use only the numbers in their ranges: text and empty cells are passed over. They take any number of ranges and values: vsum($2, $4, 10).

    | student | score | rank |
|---------+-------+------|
| ann     |    72 |    4 |
| bob     |    95 |    1 |
| cy      |    88 |    2 |
| dee     |    72 |    4 |
| eve     |    81 |    3 |
#+TBLFM: $3=vrank($2,$2)

    Ann and Dee share 4th place, and nobody is 5th: as in a spreadsheet.

    | x     |      |
|-------+------|
| 2     |      |
| 4     |      |
| 4     |      |
| 4     |      |
| 5     |      |
| 5     |      |
| 7     |      |
| 9     |      |
|-------+------|
| mean  |    5 |
| sdev  | 2.14 |
| psdev |    2 |
| mode  |    4 |
| p90   | 7.60 |
| q1    |    4 |
#+TBLFM: @10$2=vmean(@2$1..@9$1)::@11$2=vsdev(@2$1..@9$1);%.2f::@12$2=vpsdev(@2$1..@9$1)::@13$2=vmode(@2$1..@9$1)::@14$2=vpercentile(@2$1..@9$1,0.9);%.2f::@15$2=vquartile(@2$1..@9$1,1)
    Choosing: if, and, or
    Function Gives
    if(condition, then, else) then when condition is true, else otherwise; with no else, an empty cell
    and(...), or(...) true when every / any argument is true
    xor(...) true when an odd number of arguments are true
    not(x) the opposite
    iferror(value, fallback) fallback when value is not a usable number (see below), else value
    isblank(x) true for an empty cell
    isnumber(x), istext(x), isdate(x) what the cell was read as (see What a cell's value is)

    True is: true, a number other than 0, or the text t=/=true. Anything else, an empty cell included, is false. and and or given a range (and(@2$5..@9$5)) look at every cell in it.

    | name | score | grade | passed | note         |
|------+-------+-------+--------+--------------|
| ann  |    93 | A     | true   | top marks    |
| bob  |    81 | B     | true   |              |
| cy   |    58 | C     | false  | needs resit  |
#+TBLFM: $3=if($2>=90,'A',if($2>=80,'B','C'))::$4=$2>=60::$5=if($2>=90,'top marks',if($2<60,'needs resit'))

    Two things that differ from a spreadsheet:

    • Both branches of if are worked out, then one is kept. So if($2>0, 10/$2, 0) still divides by zero when $2 is 0 (harmlessly: the answer is infinity, and the 0 is kept), but a branch that is an error, like index past the end, stops the formula even when it is not the branch chosen.
    • iferror only catches bad numbers: not-a-number (0/0, sqrt(-1)), infinity (1/0) and a missing value. A function that fails (a date that cannot be read, index out of range) stops the formula before iferror is reached.
    | spent | budget | used | used, safe |
|-------+--------+------+------------|
|    50 |    200 | 0.25 |       0.25 |
|    10 |      0 | +Inf |          - |
#+TBLFM: $3=$1/$2::$4=iferror($1/$2,'-')
    Text
    Function Gives
    concat(a, b, ...) this row's values joined with nothing between: concat($1, '-', $2); a rectangle (@2$1..@4$1) gives all its cells
    join(sep, values, ...) the non-empty values joined with sep between; $1 is the whole column: join(', ', $1)
    len(text) the number of characters
    upper(text), lower(text) in capitals, in small letters
    trim(text) spaces taken off both ends, and runs of spaces inside squeezed to one
    left(text, n), right(text, n) the first or last n characters; n defaults to 1
    mid(text, start, n) n characters from start, counting the first character as 1
    substitute(text, old, new) every old replaced by new
    rept(text, n) text n times: rept('*', $2) draws a bar
    contains(text, part) true when part is in text, ignoring case
    startswith(text, part), endswith(text, part) ignoring case
    value(text) the first number in text, commas ignored: 'USD 1,234.50' is 1234.5; 0 if none
    fmt(pattern, a, b, ...) printf: fmt('%.1f%%', $2), fmt('%03d', $1), fmt('%s: %d', $1, $2)

    Numbers in text come out short (3, 2.5); dates as <2026-10-02 Fri>. In fmt, %d, %x, %o, %b and %c are given a whole number, so %d of 3.0 is 3.

    | first | last     | code | bar  | label         | t?    |
|-------+----------+------+------+---------------+-------|
| Ada   | Lovelace | ALOV | ***  | Lovelace, Ada | false |
| alan  | turing   | ATUR | **** | Turing, Alan  | true  |
#+TBLFM: $3=upper(concat(left($1),left($2,3)))::$4=rept('*',len($1))::$5=concat(upper(left($2)),mid($2,2,99),', ',upper(left($1)),mid($1,2,99))::$6=startswith($2,'T')
    Rounding and numbers
    Function Gives
    round(x), round(x, places) to the nearest; halves go away from zero. places may be negative: round(1234,-2) is 1200
    roundup(x [, places]) away from zero: roundup(2.01) is 3, roundup(-2.01) is -3
    rounddown(x [, places]) toward zero: rounddown(2.99) is 2, rounddown(-2.99) is -2
    floor(x), ceil(x) down, up (floor(-2.5) is -3)
    trunc(x), int(x) the fraction dropped
    abs(x), neg(x), sign(x) size, negated, -1 / 0 / 1
    clamp(x, low, high) x, but no lower than low and no higher than high
    mod(a, b) what is left of a after taking out bs; keeps a's sign: mod(-7,3) is -1
    rem(a, b) IEEE remainder, to the nearest multiple: rem(7,4) is -1 (use mod)
    pow(a, b), sqrt(x), exp(x), log(x) (natural), log10, log2, pow10(n), exp2(n)
    sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, and the h forms in radians; radians(deg) and degrees(rad) convert
    rand(), randint(low, high) a fraction from 0 to 1; a whole number from low to high, both possible

    Rounding is of the number itself; the ;%.2f format only changes how it is written. Rounding to places works in binary, so a value like 2.345 (stored as 2.34499…) rounds to 2.34, as it does in most languages.

    | x     | round | 1 place | up   | down | clamp |
|-------+-------+---------+------+------+-------|
| 2.375 |     2 |     2.4 |    3 |    2 | 2.375 |
| -1.25 |    -1 |    -1.3 |   -2 |   -1 |     0 |
| 17    |    17 |      17 |   17 |   17 |    10 |
#+TBLFM: $2=round($1)::$3=round($1,1)::$4=roundup($1)::$5=rounddown($1)::$6=clamp($1,0,10)
    Dates
    Function Gives
    today() today's date, no time
    now() this moment
    date(text) the date written in text
    date(year, month, day) that date; too large a day or month rolls on: date(2026,2,30) is 2 March
    days(end, start) the number of days from start to end (end first, like DAYS)
    datedif(start, end, unit) the time between, in unit: 'd' days, 'w' whole weeks, 'm' whole months, 'y' whole years. Negative when end is first
    adddays(date, n) n days on (back when negative)
    addmonths(date, n) n months on, on the same day; on a shorter month, its last day: 31 Jan + 1 is 28 Feb. edate is the same
    addyears(date, n) n years on; 29 Feb becomes 28 Feb
    addtime(date, duration) a duration on: '2h', '1d 4h', '1:30', a duration cell, or a number of minutes
    eomonth(date [, n]) the last day of the month, n months on
    workday(date, n) n working days on (Monday to Friday); back when n is negative. Holidays are not known
    networkdays(start, end) working days from start to end, both counted
    year, month, day, hour, minute (date) the part as a number
    monthname(date), weekdayname(date) January, Monday
    weekday(date) 0 for Sunday to 6 for Saturday
    yearday(date) 1 to 366
    weeknum(date) the ISO week: weeks start on Monday, week 1 holds the first Thursday
    quarter(date) 1 to 4
    datefmt(date, pattern) the date written your way (below)
    duration(text) the text read as a duration

    Days are counted by the calendar: from 23:00 one day to 01:00 the next is one day. A date argument can be a date cell, a text date ('2026-10-02'), or a number of seconds since 1970.

    datefmt uses the codes Emacs' format-time-string uses:

    Code Gives Code Gives
    %Y 2026 %H hour 00-23
    %y 26 %I hour 01-12
    %m 10 %M minutes
    %d 02 %S seconds
    %e 2 (padded) %p AM or PM
    %b Oct %a Fri
    %B October %A Friday
    %j day of year %V ISO week
    %% a % sign %Z, %z time zone 
    | task   | start            | due        | days | workdays | month end        | label      |
|--------+------------------+------------+------+----------+------------------+------------|
| report | <2026-01-30 Fri> | 2026-02-13 |   14 |       11 | <2026-02-28 Sat> | Fri 13 Feb |
| audit  | <2026-01-31 Sat> | 2026-03-31 |   59 |       42 | <2026-03-31 Tue> | Tue 31 Mar |
#+TBLFM: $4=days($3,$2)::$5=networkdays($2,$3)::$6=eomonth($3)::$7=datefmt($3,'%a %d %b')

    More:

    | date             | answer                 | how                      |
|------------------+------------------------+--------------------------|
| <2026-01-31 Sat> | <2026-02-28 Sat>       | one month on             |
| <2026-01-31 Sat> | <2026-02-02 Mon>       | next working day         |
| <2026-01-31 Sat> | <2026-01-31 Sat 02:30> | two and a half hours on  |
| <2026-01-31 Sat> | 5                      | ISO week                 |
| <2026-01-31 Sat> | 1                      | whole months to 1 March  |
#+TBLFM: @2$2=addmonths(@2$1,1)::@3$2=workday(@3$1,1)::@4$2=addtime(@4$1,'2:30')::@5$2=weeknum(@5$1)::@6$2=datedif(@6$1,'2026-03-01','m')
    Money

    These follow the spreadsheet convention: money you pay out is negative, money you receive is positive. A loan of 200000 that you receive gives a negative payment. rate is per period: a yearly 5% paid monthly is 0.05/12, with the number of periods in months. The optional type is 1 when payments are made at the start of each period, 0 (the default) at the end.

    Function Gives
    pmt(rate, nper, pv [, fv [, type]]) the payment each period that turns pv into fv (default 0)
    pv(rate, nper, pmt [, fv [, type]]) what a run of payments is worth today
    fv(rate, nper, pmt [, pv [, type]]) what you will have after nper periods
    nper(rate, pmt, pv [, fv [, type]]) how many periods it takes
    npv(rate, v1, v2, ...) today's value of amounts arriving at the end of periods 1, 2, …
    irr(v0, v1, v2, ...) the rate at which those amounts, the first one now, are worth nothing today; needs both a negative and a positive amount 
    | loan   | yearly rate | years | monthly  | total paid |  interest |
|--------+-------------+-------+----------+------------+-----------|
| 200000 |        0.05 |    30 | -1073.64 | -386511.57 | 186511.57 |
|  15000 |        0.07 |     5 |  -297.02 |  -17821.08 |   2821.08 |
#+TBLFM: $4=pmt($2/12,$3*12,$1);%.2f::$5=pmt($2/12,$3*12,$1)*$3*12;%.2f::$6=-$5-$1;%.2f

    The total is worked out from the payment itself, not from the rounded -297.02 in the cell: $5=$4*$3*12 would read back the rounded text and give -17821.20.

    | question                                  |    answer |
|-------------------------------------------+-----------|
| save 200 a month for 10 months at 6%      |   2045.61 |
| months to save 10000 at 100 a month, 12%  |     69.66 |
| 500 a month for 20 years at 8%, worth now | -59777.15 |
| npv at 10%: -10000 then 3000, 4200, 6800  |   1188.44 |
| irr of -70000 then 12000 ... 26000, in %  |      8.66 |
#+TBLFM: @2$2=fv(0.06/12,10,-200);%.2f::@3$2=nper(0.12/12,-100,0,10000);%.2f::@4$2=pv(0.08/12,12*20,500);%.2f::@5$2=npv(0.1,-10000,3000,4200,6800);%.2f::@6$2=irr(-70000,12000,15000,18000,21000,26000)*100;%.2f
    Lists

    A few functions give a list of values rather than one: sort, rsort (largest first), rdup (repeats removed, first kept), rev (reversed) and lookupall. A list written into a cell looks like [1 2 3], so they are usually wrapped in join, or given to a function that takes a range.

    | x | sorted  | unique | total of unique |
|---+---------+--------+-----------------|
| 3 | 1 2 3 3 | 3 1 2  |               6 |
| 1 |         |        |                 |
| 3 |         |        |                 |
| 2 |         |        |                 |
#+TBLFM: @2$2=join(' ',sort($1))::@2$3=join(' ',rdup($1))::@2$4=vsum(rdup($1))

    A list can only be the last argument of a function. The expression parser flattens a list that comes first into the arguments after it: join(' ', sort($1)) is fine, index(sort($1), 2) is not (the 2 becomes one more list item, and index sees five arguments).

    Other tables: remote

    remote(Name, ref) reads from the table named Name (by #+NAME: above it), looked for in the same file first and then in every other file. ref is any reference: $2 a column, @3$2 one cell, @2$1..@>$3 a block.

    #+NAME: Hits
| who | damage |
|-----+--------|
| orc |      5 |
| elf |      7 |
| orc |     12 |
    | monster | total damage | last hit | hits |
|---------+--------------+----------+------|
| orc     |           17 |       12 |    2 |
| elf     |            7 |        7 |    1 |
#+TBLFM: $2=vsumif(remote(Hits,$1),$1,remote(Hits,$2))::$3=lookuplast($1,remote(Hits,$1),remote(Hits,$2))::$4=vcountif(remote(Hits,$1),$1)

    Write the name without quotes. remote('Hits', $2) is not recognised and the formula fails.

    Colouring cells

    highlight(cell, color[, value]) writes value (or the cell's own value) and gives the cell a colour; red(cell[, value]), green, yellow, blue, cyan, purple, orange and pink are the same with the colour in the name. gradient(cell, progress, color, color...) picks a colour along the list by progress from 0 to 100.

    | task   | done | status   |
|--------+------+----------|
| write  |   90 | on track |
| review |   20 | behind   |
#+TBLFM: $3=if($2 >= 50, green($3, "on track"), red($3, "behind"))

    $2=gradient($2, $2, "red", "yellow", "green") colours a column of percentages by their own value, leaving the numbers as they are.

    The colours are not written into the file - org has nowhere to keep them. POST /table/calc answers with them beside the table, and an editor (the vscode plugin) shows them until the table is next changed.

    Spreadsheet names

    For finding the function you would have used in a spreadsheet:

    Spreadsheet Here Spreadsheet Here
    SUM, AVERAGE, MEDIAN vsum, vmean, vmedian IF, AND, OR, NOT if, and, or, not
    MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTA vmin, vmax, vcount, vcounta IFERROR iferror (numbers only)
    COUNTBLANK, PRODUCT vcountblank, vprod ISBLANK, ISNUMBER isblank, isnumber
    SUMIF, COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF vsumif, vcountif, vmeanif CONCAT, TEXTJOIN concat, join
    SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS vsumifs, vcountifs, vmeanifs LEN, UPPER, LOWER len, upper, lower
    MAXIFS, MINIFS vmaxif, vminif (one criterion) LEFT, RIGHT, MID left, right, mid
    VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP lookup TRIM, SUBSTITUTE trim, substitute
    INDEX, MATCH index, match REPT, VALUE, TEXT rept, value, fmt / datefmt
    STDEV, STDEV.P, VAR, VAR.P vsdev, vpsdev, vvar, vpvar SEARCH (as a test) contains
    MODE, PERCENTILE, QUARTILE vmode, vpercentile, vquartile TODAY, NOW, DATE today, now, date
    RANK vrank DAYS, DATEDIF days, datedif
    ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN round, roundup, rounddown EDATE, EOMONTH addmonths, eomonth
    INT, ABS, SIGN, MOD floor, abs, sign, mod WORKDAY, NETWORKDAYS workday, networkdays
    RAND, RANDBETWEEN rand, randint WEEKNUM, WEEKDAY weeknum (ISO), weekday
    PMT, PV, FV, NPER, NPV, IRR the same, in small letters YEAR, MONTH, DAY year, month, day

    Spreadsheet INT rounds down, which is floor here; int here drops the fraction, which differs for negative numbers.

    Things that catch you out
    • $2 is a column or a cell depending on the function. Ranges for vsum and friends, one cell for sqrt and friends. See How a function reads its arguments.
    • A whole column includes everything under the header, summary rows too. Under a total row, use @2$3..@5$3 rather than $3.
    • Rows are counted without separator lines.
    • Both branches of if are worked out. An error in either stops the formula.
    • iferror catches bad numbers, not errors.
    • A list can only be the last argument. join(',', sort($1)), never index(sort($1), 1).
    • Cell references are found inside quotes too. '$1' in a formula becomes a reference to column 1, so it cannot be written as text (value('USD 1,234') works; value('$1,234') does not).
    • remote takes the table name without quotes.
    • Constants are text: value($vat), not $vat.
    • A week is five days in a duration (1w is 5d), as for effort estimates.
    • rem is not mod: rem(7,4) is -1.
    • Formulas don't run on their own. Run them with orgs tables eval, worg or VS Code.

    Table Functions

    Orgs cannot support the more rigorous org mode like table syntax. It does it's best but a true implementation of org mode table syntax would require that orgs run a lisp interpreter inside your editor, and that's just not possible. That said, orgs does facilitate a very robust table evaluation that I hope might prove useful to people other than just me.

    Here is an example of a table with some expressions. org mode stores all table expression at the end of a table in a TBLFM: comment.

    #+NAME: Monsters
| Monster Name | Start Health | Total Damage | %Alive | AC | Initiative |
|--------------+--------------+--------------+--------+----+------------|
| M1           |           44 |            0 |  100.0 |    |            |
#+TBLFM:$4=(($2-$3)/$2)*100.0;%.1f::$3=lookuplast($1,remote(FightHistory,$2),remote(FightHistory,$4))

    Looking at the first operation (up to the ::)

    	$4=(($2-$3)/$2)*100.0;%.1f

    This states that every entry in the 4th column (IE the %Alive column) is set to the (Start Health - Total Damage) / Start Health * 100.0 So each monsters % alive is the percentage of health left.

    Then there is that funny %.1f which tells the system to only keep one decimal place becase more would be tedious to look at.

    Next $3 finds the last row of the FightHistory table whose 2nd column holds my Monster Name, and pulls the value from its 4th column. This means I can update the fight history table and have this table auto update from it. To total every hit instead of taking the last one:

    	$3=vsumif(remote(FightHistory,$2),$1,remote(FightHistory,$4))

    The full guide, with a worked example for every function (each one run by the test suite), is docs/tables.org. What follows is the short reference.

    How functions read their arguments

    A range argument is expanded in full: in vsum($2) or vcountif($2,'>3'), $2 is the whole column (the header row is skipped). A value argument reads one cell: in sqrt($2) or the first argument of lookup($1,...), $2 is the cell in the current row.

    Strings may use single or double quotes. A cell reference inside a string is still replaced, so a literal like '$1' cannot be written.

    A function returning a list (sort, rsort, rdup, rev, lookupall) can only be the last argument of another function: join(',', sort($1)) works, index(sort($1), 2) does not.

    Criteria (the vsumif / vcountif family) are a value meaning "equal to", or a string starting with an operator: '>10', '<=2026-01-01', '<>done', '=' (empty), '<>' (not empty). Text compares without regard to case, and * and ? are wildcards: 'app*'.

    Conditional aggregates

    vsumif(range, criteria [, values])
    sum of values (or of range) where range meets criteria
    vcountif(range, criteria)
    count of cells meeting criteria
    vmeanif, vmaxif, vminif (range, criteria [, values])
    as vsumif
    vsumifs(values, range1, criteria1, range2, criteria2, …)
    sum where every criterion holds
    vmeanifs(values, range1, criteria1, …), vcountifs(range1, criteria1, …)
    as vsumifs
    vcounta(range)
    non-empty cells
    vcountblank(range)
    empty cells

    Lookups

    lookup(value, keys [, results])
    the result beside the first key equal to value, empty when none; lookupfirst is the same
    lookuplast(value, keys [, results])
    the last match instead
    lookupall(value, keys [, results])
    every match, as a list: join(', ', lookupall($1, …))
    index(range, n)
    the nth cell from 1; -1 is the last
    match(value, range)
    position of the first equal cell from 1, 0 when none

    With no results range, lookups return the matching key, as org-lookup-first does.

    vpsdev, vpvar

    p from 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100), interpolated like PERCENTILE.INC
    vquartile(range, q)

    vrank(value, range [, ascending])

    payment per period: pmt(0.05/12, 360, 200000) is -1073.64
